questionText: How many diameters of a circle can be drawn from one point on the circle?
hints: Think about what makes a line a diameter. It has to pass through one special point of the circle.
A diameter starts on the circle, passes through the centre, and ends on the circle. From your point, how many straight lines go through the centre?

Similar example: how many radii can be drawn from the centre of a circle? A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle. There are endless points on the circle, so endless radii can be drawn from the centre.

stepByStep.text: A diameter is a straight line that joins two points on the circle and passes through the centre.
Start at the chosen point on the circle. To be a diameter, the line must go straight through the centre.
Only one straight line can pass through two fixed points, here the chosen point and the centre.
So only 1 diameter can be drawn from a point on the circle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! A diameter must pass through the centre, and only one straight line joins your point to the centre and carries on to the other side.
misconceptions.B: Other lines from the point miss the centre, so they are chords, not diameters. Count only the line that passes through the centre.
misconceptions.C: Many chords can be drawn from one point, but a diameter must pass through the centre. Only one line from the point does that.
misconceptions.D: A whole circle has endless diameters, but each one starts from a different point. From one point, only one line goes through the centre.

questionText: Area of circle = 3× circumference. Radius?
hints: This is a circle problem that uses two formulas: area = π × r × r and circumference = 2 × π × r. Compare the two.
Write 3 times the circumference: 3 × 2 × π × r. Then set it beside the area, π × r × r, and see what r must be.

Similar example: the area of a circle is 2 times its circumference. 2 times the circumference is 2 × 2 × π × r, which is 4 × π × r. The area is π × r × r. Both have π × r, so the other r must be 4. The radius is 4.

stepByStep.text: The area of a circle is π × r × r. The circumference is 2 × π × r.
3 times the circumference is 3 × 2 × π × r, which is 6 × π × r.
So π × r × r is the same as 6 × π × r. Both sides have π × r, so the r that is left must equal 6.
The radius is 6.

misconceptions.A: Try it: with radius 5 the area is 25 × π and 3 times the circumference is 30 × π. They are not equal.
misconceptions.B: Yes! With radius 6 the area is 36 × π and 3 times the circumference is also 36 × π.
misconceptions.C: Try it: with radius 7 the area is 49 × π and 3 times the circumference is 42 × π. They are not equal.
misconceptions.D: Try it: with radius 8 the area is 64 × π and 3 times the circumference is 48 × π. They are not equal.

questionText: Circumference and area of circle are numerically same. Diameter?
hints: This is a circle problem with two formulas: circumference = 2 × π × r and area = π × r × r. Compare them, and read carefully whether the radius or the diameter is asked.
Set 2 × π × r beside π × r × r. Both have π × r. See what the remaining r must be, and remember the question asks for the diameter.

Similar example: the area of a circle is 5 times its circumference. 5 times the circumference is 5 × 2 × π × r, which is 10 × π × r. The area is π × r × r, so r must be 10. The diameter is 2 × 10 = 20.

stepByStep.text: The circumference is 2 × π × r. The area is π × r × r.
They are equal. Both have π × r, so the r that is left must equal 2. The radius is 2 cm.
The diameter is twice the radius.
The diameter is 4 cm.

misconceptions.A: Try it: a diameter of 6 cm gives radius 3 cm. Then the circumference is 6 × π and the area is 9 × π, which are not equal.
misconceptions.B: 2 cm is the radius. The question asks for the diameter, which is twice as long.
misconceptions.C: Yes! With radius 2 cm, the circumference and the area are both 4 × π, and the diameter is 4 cm.
misconceptions.D: There is a value that fits. Find the radius first, then double it.

questionText: Eight equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 4. Each circle touches the circles next to it and the nearest sides of the rectangle at one point only. The radius of each circle is 7 cm. What is the area of the rectangle?
hints: The circles fill the rectangle exactly, so its length and breadth can be counted in circle widths. The width of a circle is its diameter.
Find the diameter of one circle: it is twice the radius of 7 cm. The length of the rectangle is 4 diameters and the breadth is 2 diameters.

Similar example: 10 equal circles of radius 2 cm sit in a rectangle in 2 rows of 5. The diameter is 4 cm. The length is 5 × 4 = 20 cm and the breadth is 2 × 4 = 8 cm, so the area is 20 × 8 = 160 sq cm.

stepByStep.text: The diameter of each circle is twice the radius.
The length holds 4 circles side by side.
The breadth holds 2 circles.
Area is length times breadth. The area of the rectangle is 1568 sq.cm.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The diameter is 14 cm, so the rectangle is 56 cm by 28 cm, and 56 × 28 = 1568.
misconceptions.B: The sides may be right, so check the multiplying. 56 × 20 = 1120 and 56 × 8 = 448. Add these two.
misconceptions.C: 784 is 28 × 28, which uses a length of only 2 diameters. The length holds 4 circles, so it is 4 × 14 = 56 cm.
misconceptions.D: This is a little too big. Try 56 × 28 in two parts, 56 × 20 and 56 × 8, then add them.

questionText: Circumference of circle = 132cm. Find area.
hints: This is a circle problem in two parts. Use the circumference to find the radius, then use the radius to find the area. Take π as 22/7.
Circumference = 2 × π × r. Put 132 for the circumference and 22/7 for π, and find r.
Similar example: a circle has circumference 44 cm. With π as 22/7, the circumference is 44/7 times r, so r is 44 × 7 ÷ 44 = 7 cm. The area is 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154 sq. cm.

stepByStep.text: Circumference = 2 × π × r. With π as 22/7, this is 44/7 times r.
So r is 132 × 7 ÷ 44. The radius is 21 cm.
Area = π × r × r.
The area is 1386 sq. cm.

misconceptions.A: Check the last multiplication. With radius 21 cm, 22/7 × 21 × 21 is the same as 22 × 3 × 21.
misconceptions.B: The radius is 21 cm. Work out 22 × 63 again carefully.
misconceptions.C: Find the radius first: 132 × 7 ÷ 44 = 21 cm. Then use area = π × r × r.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The radius is 21 cm, and 22/7 × 21 × 21 = 1386.

questionText: Circle circumference = perimeter of rectangle (14cm×8cm). Radius?
hints: This problem joins two shapes. Find the perimeter of the rectangle first, then use the circumference formula, 2 × π × r, with π as 22/7.
Work out the perimeter of the rectangle: 2 times (length + breadth). That number is also the circumference of the circle.

Similar example: a circle's circumference equals the perimeter of a rectangle 50 cm by 38 cm. The perimeter is 2 × (50 + 38) = 176 cm. With π as 22/7, the circumference is 44/7 times r, so r is 176 × 7 ÷ 44 = 28 cm.

stepByStep.text: Find the perimeter of the rectangle.
The circumference is also 44 cm. Circumference = 2 × π × r, which is 44/7 times r when π is 22/7.
The radius is 7 cm.

misconceptions.A: 14 cm is the diameter of this circle. The radius is half of it.
misconceptions.B: Check the perimeter first: 2 × (14 + 8) = 44 cm. Then find r from the circumference formula.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The perimeter is 44 cm, and a circle of radius 7 cm has circumference 44 cm.
misconceptions.D: This halves once too often. The radius is 7 cm, and 3.5 cm is half of the radius.

questionText: The distance from the centre of a circle to any point on the circle is called the:
hints: This is about the parts of a circle. Each part has its own name. Think about which one starts at the centre.
Picture a line drawn from the centre straight out to the edge of the circle. It goes only halfway across.
Similar example: a line that joins two points on a circle and passes through the centre goes all the way across. It is called the diameter.

stepByStep.text: Mark the centre of a circle and any point on the circle.
The line joining them goes from the centre to the edge. Every such line has the same length.
This distance is called the Radius.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The radius is the distance from the centre to the circle.
misconceptions.B: A diameter goes all the way across the circle through the centre. From the centre to the circle is only half of that.
misconceptions.C: A chord joins two points on the circle. This distance starts at the centre.
misconceptions.D: The circumference is the distance all the way around the circle.

questionText: The diameter of a circle is:
hints: This is about the parts of a circle. Think about how the radius and the diameter are drawn.
Draw a diameter and mark the centre on it. Count how many radii lie along that diameter.
Similar example: a circle has diameter 12 cm. The centre cuts the diameter into two equal pieces, and each piece is a radius. So the radius is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.

stepByStep.text: A diameter goes across the circle through the centre.
The centre cuts it into two pieces, and each piece is a radius.
So the diameter is Twice the radius.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Two radii placed end to end through the centre make a diameter.
misconceptions.B: It is the other way round: the radius is half the diameter.
misconceptions.C: The radius reaches only from the centre to the circle. The diameter goes right across.
misconceptions.D: Only two radii fit along a diameter, one on each side of the centre.

questionText: The longest chord of a circle is the:
hints: This is about the parts of a circle. A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle.
Picture chords drawn across a circle. They get longer as they move closer to the centre. Where is the longest one?
Similar example: in a circle with centre O, chord PQ passes through O and chord RS does not. PQ is made of two radii end to end, so it is as long as a chord can be. RS is shorter.

stepByStep.text: A chord joins two points on the circle.
Chords get longer as they get closer to the centre. The longest one passes through the centre.
A chord through the centre is called a diameter. So the longest chord is the Diameter.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The chord through the centre is the longest, and it is the diameter.
misconceptions.B: A radius goes from the centre to the circle, so it is not a chord. A chord joins two points on the circle.
misconceptions.C: An arc is a curved piece of the circle itself. A chord is a straight line.
misconceptions.D: A tangent touches the circle at just one point from outside. A chord joins two points on the circle.

questionText: If the radius of a circle is 7 cm, what is its diameter?
hints: This is about the radius and the diameter of a circle. Think about how the two are related.
The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre, so it is made of two radii. Use the radius of 7 cm.
Similar example: a circle has radius 9 cm. The diameter is twice the radius, so it is 2 × 9 = 18 cm.

stepByStep.text: The diameter is twice the radius.
Multiply the radius by 2.
The diameter is 14 cm.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The diameter is twice the radius, and 2 × 7 = 14.
misconceptions.B: This is half of the radius. The diameter is bigger than the radius, so multiply by 2.
misconceptions.C: This is 3 times the radius. A diameter is made of 2 radii.
misconceptions.D: This is 7 × 7. For the diameter, multiply the radius by 2.

questionText: The boundary of a circle is called the:
hints: This question is about the names of the parts of a circle. Think about which word means the line that goes all the way around.
Picture walking along the edge of a round park until you are back where you started. Which word names that whole path around?
A similar example: the line going all the way around a square is called its perimeter. A circle has its own special word for the distance all the way around.

stepByStep.text: The boundary of a circle is the curved line that goes all the way around it.
The length of that line has a special name. It is like a perimeter, but for a circle.
The boundary of a circle is called the circumference.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The circumference is the line all the way around a circle.
misconceptions.B: Area is the space inside the circle, not its edge. Think of the line that goes around.
misconceptions.C: The diameter is a straight line across the circle through the centre. The boundary is the curved line around it.
misconceptions.D: The radius goes from the centre to the edge. The boundary is the curved line all the way around.

questionText: The diameter of a circular plate is 18 cm. What is its radius?
hints: Think about how the radius and the diameter of a circle are related.
The radius is half of the diameter. Find half of 18.
Example: A circle has diameter 10 cm. Its radius is 10 divided by 2 = 5 cm.

stepByStep.text: The radius goes from the centre to the circle. The diameter goes right across through the centre, so it is two radii.
Halve the diameter.
The radius is 9 cm.

misconceptions.A: This doubles 18. Doubling turns a radius into a diameter; here you need to go from diameter to radius, so halve.
misconceptions.B: The radius is shorter than the diameter. It is exactly half of it.
misconceptions.C: This divides 18 by 3. A diameter is made of 2 radii, so divide by 2.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Half of 18 cm is 9 cm.

questionText: Kiran wants to draw a circle of diameter 12 cm with a compass. How far apart should the needle point and the pencil tip be?
hints: The needle of a compass sits at the centre and the pencil draws the circle. Think about which length that is.
The opening of the compass is the radius. Find the radius of a circle whose diameter is 12 cm.
Example: For a circle of diameter 20 cm, the compass is opened to the radius, 20 divided by 2 = 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: The needle is at the centre and the pencil is on the circle, so the opening of the compass is the radius.
The radius is half the diameter.
The needle point and pencil tip should be 6 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The compass is opened to the radius, and half of 12 cm is 6 cm.
misconceptions.B: An opening of 12 cm would give a circle 24 cm across. The compass is opened to the radius, not the diameter.
misconceptions.C: This doubles 12. The compass opening is the radius, which is half of the diameter.
misconceptions.D: This halves 12 twice. Halve only once to go from diameter to radius.

questionText: A circle has a radius of 8 cm. How long is the longest chord that can be drawn in this circle?
hints: A chord joins two points on a circle. Think about which chord is the longest of all.
The longest chord passes through the centre, so it is the diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 8 cm.
Example: In a circle of radius 5 cm, the longest chord is the diameter, 2 x 5 = 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: The longest chord of a circle is the one through the centre, which is the diameter.
The diameter is twice the radius.
The longest chord is 16 cm.

misconceptions.A: 8 cm is the radius. The longest chord goes right across the circle through the centre.
misconceptions.B: That is right! The longest chord is the diameter, 16 cm.
misconceptions.C: This halves the radius. The longest chord is the diameter, which is twice the radius.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 8 by 8. The longest chord is the diameter, 2 times the radius.

questionText: A circle has a radius of 6 cm. Point P is 4 cm away from the centre of the circle. Where is point P?

options.text: At the centre of the circle

hints: Every point on a circle is exactly one radius away from the centre. Compare the point's distance with the radius.
Is 4 cm less than, equal to, or more than the radius of 6 cm?
Example: A circle has radius 5 cm and a point is 9 cm from the centre. Since 9 is more than 5, that point is outside the circle.

stepByStep.text: Points on the circle are exactly 6 cm from the centre.
Point P is 4 cm from the centre, and 4 is less than 6.
A point closer to the centre than the radius lies inside the circle, so P is inside the circle.

misconceptions.A: A point on the circle would be exactly 6 cm from the centre. P is only 4 cm away.
misconceptions.B: A point outside the circle would be more than 6 cm from the centre. P is only 4 cm away.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 4 cm is less than the radius of 6 cm, so P is inside the circle.
misconceptions.D: The centre is 0 cm away from itself. P is 4 cm away from the centre, so it is not at the centre.

questionText: O is the centre of a circle. A and B are two different points on the circle. If OA = 7 cm, how long is OB?
hints: Think about what kind of line joins the centre of a circle to a point on the circle.
OA and OB both go from the centre to the circle, so both are radii. What do you know about all the radii of one circle?
Example: In a circle with centre C, if CP = 4 cm and Q is also on the circle, then CQ is also a radius, so CQ = 4 cm.

stepByStep.text: OA joins the centre to a point on the circle, so OA is a radius.
OB also joins the centre to a point on the circle, so OB is a radius too.
All radii of a circle are equal, so OB = 7 cm.

misconceptions.A: 14 cm is the diameter. OB stops at the centre, so it is a radius.
misconceptions.B: This halves the radius. OB is a full radius, just like OA.
misconceptions.C: This is three radii. OB is one radius, just like OA.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Every radius of the same circle has the same length, 7 cm.

questionText: Four equal circles, each of radius 3 cm, are drawn in a straight row so that each circle touches the next one. What is the distance from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last circle?
hints: When two equal circles touch, think about how far apart their centres are.
The centres of two touching circles are one radius plus one radius apart. Find that distance for radius 3 cm.
Example: Three circles of radius 2 cm touch in a row. Neighbouring centres are 4 cm apart, and there are 2 gaps from first to last, so the distance is 2 x 4 = 8 cm.

stepByStep.text: Centres of neighbouring circles are two radii apart.
From the first centre to the fourth centre there are 3 gaps.
Multiply.
The distance between the first and last centres is 18 cm.

misconceptions.A: Great thinking! 3 gaps of 6 cm make 18 cm.
misconceptions.B: This is the full length of the row, 4 diameters. From centre to centre, half a circle is left out at each end.
misconceptions.C: This multiplies 4 circles by the radius. Count the gaps between centres: there are 3, each 6 cm.
misconceptions.D: This uses 3 gaps of 3 cm. Each gap between centres is two radii, 6 cm.

questionText: Six round bangles, each of radius 4 cm, are placed in a straight row on a table so that each bangle touches the next. How long is the row from end to end?
hints: Each bangle takes up its full width in the row. Think about which length of a circle is its width.
The width of one bangle is its diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 4 cm.
Example: Five coins of radius 1 cm in a row. Each coin is 2 cm wide, so the row is 5 x 2 = 10 cm long.

stepByStep.text: Each bangle is one diameter wide.
There are 6 bangles in the row.
The row is 48 cm long.

misconceptions.A: This uses the radius as the width. Each bangle is a full diameter, 8 cm, wide.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 6 bangles, each 8 cm wide, make 48 cm.
misconceptions.C: This counts 5 gaps between centres. From end to end, all 6 full bangles are counted.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the diameter again. Each bangle is 8 cm wide, and there are 6 of them.

questionText: A circle is drawn inside a square of side 10 cm so that it just touches all four sides of the square. What is the radius of the circle?
hints: Picture the circle fitting snugly in the square. Think about which length of the circle stretches from one side of the square to the opposite side.
The circle reaches from one side to the opposite side, so its diameter equals the side of the square, 10 cm.
Example: A circle just fits in a square of side 8 cm. Its diameter is 8 cm, so its radius is 4 cm.

stepByStep.text: The circle touches opposite sides of the square, so its diameter equals the side of the square.
The diameter is 10 cm.
The radius is half the diameter.
The radius of the circle is 5 cm.

misconceptions.A: 10 cm is the diameter of the circle. The radius is half of that.
misconceptions.B: This doubles the side. The side of the square equals the diameter, and the radius is half of it.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The diameter is 10 cm, so the radius is 5 cm.
misconceptions.D: This is the perimeter of the square. The radius is half of one side.

questionText: A circle of radius 6 cm fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the perimeter of the square?
hints: First find the side of the square from the circle, then find the distance around the square.
The side of the square equals the diameter of the circle. Find the diameter when the radius is 6 cm.
Example: A circle of radius 2 cm fits exactly in a square. The side is 4 cm, so the perimeter is 4 x 4 = 16 cm.

stepByStep.text: The side of the square equals the diameter.
A square has 4 equal sides.
The perimeter of the square is 48 cm.

misconceptions.A: This uses the radius as the side. The side of the square is the diameter, 12 cm.
misconceptions.B: This is one side of the square. The perimeter is all 4 sides together.
misconceptions.C: This is the area of the square, 12 x 12. The perimeter is 4 times the side.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Each side is 12 cm, and 4 sides make 48 cm.

questionText: Two coins lie flat on a table and touch each other. The radius of one coin is 5 cm and the radius of the other is 3 cm. How far apart are their centres?
hints: Imagine a straight line from one centre to the other. It passes through the point where the coins touch.
The line goes from the first centre to the touching point (one radius), then on to the second centre (the other radius).
Example: Circles of radius 4 cm and 2 cm touch side by side. Their centres are 4 + 2 = 6 cm apart.

stepByStep.text: The line joining the centres passes through the point where the coins touch.
It is made of the radius of one coin and the radius of the other.
Add the two radii.
The centres are 8 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: That is right! One radius of 5 cm and one of 3 cm make 8 cm.
misconceptions.B: This subtracts the radii. The coins lie side by side, so the two radii are added.
misconceptions.C: This adds the two diameters. From centre to centre you need only one radius of each coin.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies the radii. The distance is one radius plus the other radius.

questionText: Two circles are drawn with the same centre. The radius of the big circle is 9 cm and the radius of the small circle is 5 cm. How wide is the ring between the two circles?
hints: Walk in a straight line from the centre outwards. You cross the small circle first and then the big circle.
The width of the ring is how much farther the big circle is from the centre than the small circle.
Example: Circles with the same centre have radii 10 cm and 7 cm. The ring between them is 10 - 7 = 3 cm wide.

stepByStep.text: Going out from the centre, the small circle is 5 cm away and the big circle is 9 cm away.
The ring is the gap between them.
The ring is 4 cm wide.

misconceptions.A: This adds the radii. The ring is the gap between the circles, so subtract.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The big circle is 4 cm farther from the centre than the small one.
misconceptions.C: This subtracts the diameters, 18 and 10. The ring's width on one side is the difference of the radii.
misconceptions.D: This halves the gap. The ring's width is the full difference of the radii, 9 - 5.

questionText: The diameter of a circle is 12 cm longer than its radius. What is the radius of the circle?
hints: A diameter is made of two radii. Think about what is left when you take one radius away from the diameter.
Diameter = radius + radius. If the diameter is also radius + 12 cm, what must the second radius be?
Example: A diameter is 5 cm longer than its radius. Since the diameter is radius + radius, the extra part is one radius, so the radius is 5 cm.

stepByStep.text: The diameter is two radii: radius + radius.
We are told the diameter is radius + 12 cm.
Comparing the two, the second radius must be the extra 12 cm.
Check: the diameter is 24 cm, and it is 12 cm longer than the radius.
The radius is 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: This halves 12. Check it: a radius of 6 cm gives a diameter of 12 cm, which is only 6 cm longer.
misconceptions.B: 24 cm is the diameter of this circle. The question asks for the radius.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! The diameter, 24 cm, is exactly 12 cm longer than the radius, 12 cm.
misconceptions.D: This divides 12 by 3. Check it: a radius of 4 cm gives a diameter of 8 cm, which is only 4 cm longer.

questionText: A circle has a radius of 6 cm. Which of these lengths can NOT be the length of a chord of this circle?
hints: A chord joins two points on the circle. Think about how long the longest possible chord is.
The longest chord is the diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 6 cm.
Example: In a circle of radius 5 cm the longest chord is 10 cm, so a chord of 11 cm is not possible, but chords of 3 cm or 10 cm are.

stepByStep.text: The longest chord is the diameter.
So a chord can be any length up to 12 cm, but never longer.
4 cm, 9 cm and 12 cm are all possible. The length that cannot be a chord is 13 cm.

misconceptions.A: A short chord of 4 cm fits easily near the edge of the circle. Look for a length longer than the diameter.
misconceptions.B: A chord of 9 cm is shorter than the diameter of 12 cm, so it fits. Look for a length longer than the diameter.
misconceptions.C: 12 cm is exactly the diameter, which is the longest chord, so it is possible.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 13 cm is longer than the diameter of 12 cm, so no chord can be that long.

questionText: A rectangular tray is 20 cm long and 8 cm wide. Round biscuits of radius 2 cm are laid flat on it in straight rows, touching each other but not overlapping. What is the greatest number of biscuits that fit on the tray?
hints: Each round biscuit needs a square space as wide as the biscuit. Find how many fit along the length and along the width.
The width of one biscuit is its diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 2 cm.
Example: A tray 12 cm by 6 cm holds circles of radius 3 cm. Each is 6 cm wide, so 2 fit along the length and 1 along the width: 2 x 1 = 2 circles.

stepByStep.text: Each biscuit is one diameter wide.
Biscuits along the length.
Rows along the width.
Multiply.
The tray holds 10 biscuits.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 2 rows of 5 biscuits make 10.
misconceptions.B: This is one row only. The tray is 8 cm wide, so a second row of 4 cm biscuits fits too.
misconceptions.C: This uses 2 cm as the width of a biscuit across the tray. Each biscuit is a full 4 cm wide in both directions.
misconceptions.D: This uses the radius, 2 cm, as the width of a biscuit. Each biscuit is one diameter, 4 cm, wide.

questionText: A piece of wire is bent to make a circle of radius 7 cm. The same wire is straightened and bent again to make a square. What is the side of the square? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: The length of the wire does not change. It is the distance around the circle, and then the distance around the square.
Find the circumference of the circle: 2 times 22/7 times 7.
Example: A wire makes a circle of radius 14 cm. Its length is 2 x 22/7 x 14 = 88 cm. Bent into a square, each side is 88 divided by 4 = 22 cm.

stepByStep.text: The length of the wire is the circumference of the circle.
The same 44 cm of wire goes around the square.
A square has 4 equal sides.
The side of the square is 11 cm.

misconceptions.A: 44 cm is the whole length of the wire. Share it among the 4 sides of the square.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 44 cm of wire makes a square of side 11 cm.
misconceptions.C: 14 cm is the diameter of the circle. The side of the square comes from the wire's length, 44 cm, shared among 4 sides.
misconceptions.D: This divides the wire by 2. A square has 4 equal sides, so divide 44 by 4.

questionText: The radius of a big circle is equal to the diameter of a small circle. The radius of the small circle is 3 cm. What is the diameter of the big circle?
hints: Go one step at a time: small radius, small diameter, big radius, big diameter.
Find the diameter of the small circle first: twice 3 cm.
Example: A small circle has radius 2 cm, so its diameter is 4 cm. A big circle with radius 4 cm has diameter 8 cm.

stepByStep.text: Diameter of the small circle.
This is the radius of the big circle, so the big radius is 6 cm.
Diameter of the big circle.
The diameter of the big circle is 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: 6 cm is the radius of the big circle. Double it to get the big circle's diameter.
misconceptions.B: 3 cm is the radius of the small circle. Double it to get the big radius, then double again.
misconceptions.C: Well done! Doubling twice takes 3 cm to 6 cm and then to 12 cm.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 3 by 3. Each step from radius to diameter is a doubling.

questionText: Three equal circles with centres A, B and C each have a radius of 4 cm. Each circle touches the other two. What is the perimeter of triangle ABC?
hints: Each side of the triangle joins the centres of two touching circles. Find the length of one side first.
When two circles touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius: 4 + 4.
Example: Three circles of radius 5 cm touch each other. Each side of the triangle of centres is 10 cm, so its perimeter is 3 x 10 = 30 cm.

stepByStep.text: Each side joins two centres of touching circles.
The triangle has 3 such sides.
The perimeter of triangle ABC is 24 cm.

misconceptions.A: This uses 4 cm for each side. Each side is two radii, 8 cm.
misconceptions.B: 8 cm is one side of the triangle. The perimeter is all 3 sides together.
misconceptions.C: This doubles once too often. Each side is 8 cm, and 3 sides make the perimeter.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 3 sides of 8 cm make 24 cm.

questionText: Ten equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 5. Each circle touches the circles next to it, and the outer circles touch the sides of the rectangle. The perimeter of the rectangle is 84 cm. What is the radius of each circle?
hints: Write the length and the width of the rectangle as a number of diameters, then use the perimeter.
The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters. How many diameters make up half of the perimeter?
Example: Six circles in 2 rows of 3 fill a rectangle of perimeter 40 cm. Length + width = 3 + 2 = 5 diameters = 20 cm, so a diameter is 4 cm and the radius is 2 cm.

stepByStep.text: The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters.
Length + width is half the perimeter.
Length + width is 7 diameters.
The radius is half the diameter.
The radius of each circle is 3 cm.

misconceptions.A: Great work! The diameter is 6 cm, so the radius is 3 cm.
misconceptions.B: 6 cm is the diameter of each circle. The radius is half of it.
misconceptions.C: This divides the whole perimeter by 7. Only half the perimeter, 42 cm, equals 7 diameters.
misconceptions.D: This divides 84 by 4 as if the rectangle were a square. The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters.

questionText: A small circle of radius 3 cm lies inside a big circle of radius 10 cm and touches it at exactly one point. How far apart are the centres of the two circles?
hints: Draw a line from the big centre to the touching point. The small circle's centre lies on this line.
From the big centre to the touching point is 10 cm. From the small centre to the same point is 3 cm.
Example: A circle of radius 2 cm touches a circle of radius 8 cm from inside. The centres are 8 - 2 = 6 cm apart.

stepByStep.text: The big centre, the small centre and the touching point lie on one straight line.
The big centre is 10 cm from the touching point, and the small centre is 3 cm from it.
The distance between the centres is the difference.
The centres are 7 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: Adding the radii is for circles that touch side by side from outside. Here the small circle is inside the big one.
misconceptions.B: That is right! The small centre is 3 cm back from the touching point, so it is 7 cm from the big centre.
misconceptions.C: This takes away the small circle's diameter. Only its radius lies between its centre and the touching point.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies the radii. The centres are apart by the difference of the radii.

questionText: Three circles of radii 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm are drawn in a row with their centres on one straight line. The middle circle, of radius 3 cm, touches the other two. What is the distance from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last circle?
hints: Travel along the line from the first centre to the last centre and note which parts of each circle you cross.
You cross one radius of the first circle, then the whole middle circle, then one radius of the last circle.
Example: Circles of radii 1 cm, 2 cm and 5 cm in a row. From first centre to last centre: 1 + (2 + 2) + 5 = 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: From the first centre to its edge is one radius, 2 cm.
Crossing the whole middle circle is its diameter.
From the edge of the last circle to its centre is one radius, 4 cm.
Add the three parts.
The distance between the first and last centres is 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: This adds the three radii once each. The middle circle is crossed completely, so its radius is counted twice.
misconceptions.B: This is the full length of the row from end to end. From centre to centre, only one radius of each end circle is counted.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 2 + 6 + 4 = 12.
misconceptions.D: This counts the whole last circle. Stop at its centre, so count only one radius, 4 cm, for it.

questionText: The circumference of a circle is 88 cm. The circle fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the side of the square? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Work backwards from the circumference to the radius, then think about how the circle sits in the square.
Circumference = 2 times 22/7 times radius. So 44/7 times the radius is 88.
Example: A circle has circumference 44 cm. Then 44/7 times the radius is 44, so the radius is 7 cm. The square around it has side equal to the diameter, 14 cm.

stepByStep.text: The circumference is 2 times 22/7 times the radius.
So the radius is 14 cm.
The side of the square equals the diameter.
The side of the square is 28 cm.

misconceptions.A: 14 cm is the radius of the circle. The side of the square is the diameter.
misconceptions.B: This shares 88 cm among 4 sides. The 88 cm goes around the circle, not around the square.
misconceptions.C: This doubles the diameter. The side of the square is equal to one diameter.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The radius is 14 cm, so the diameter and the side of the square are 28 cm.

questionText: A circle of radius 7 cm is cut out of a square sheet of paper of side 14 cm. What is the area of the paper that is left? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: The paper left is the square with the circle taken away. Find two areas.
Find the area of the square first: 14 times 14.
Example: A circle of area 154 sq cm is cut from a square sheet of side 20 cm. The square is 400 sq cm, so 400 - 154 = 246 sq cm is left.

stepByStep.text: Area of the square.
Area of the circle.
Take the circle away from the square.
The area of paper left is 42 sq cm.

misconceptions.A: That is right! 196 - 154 = 42.
misconceptions.B: This takes away the circumference, 44, from the area of the square. Take away the area of the circle, 154.
misconceptions.C: This is the area of the circle that was cut out. The question asks for the paper left behind.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two areas. The circle is cut out, so subtract it from the square.

questionText: Five points are marked on a circle. Every pair of points is joined by a straight line. How many chords are drawn?
hints: Each chord joins two of the points. Count the pairs in an orderly way so that none is counted twice.
Call the points P, Q, R, S, T. Start by counting the chords from P to each of the other four points.
Example: With 4 points on a circle, the first point joins 3 others, the next joins 2 new ones, and the next joins 1 new one: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 chords.

stepByStep.text: From the first point, 4 chords go to the other points.
From the second point, 3 new chords can be drawn, then 2 from the third and 1 from the fourth.
Add them.
10 chords are drawn.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the chords joining neighbouring points. Points that are not neighbours are joined too.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 chords.
misconceptions.C: This counts 4 chords from each of the 5 points, but then every chord is counted twice, once from each end.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 5 by 5. A point is not joined to itself, and each chord should be counted only once.

questionText: Two square trays each have a side of 24 cm. The first tray is exactly filled by 9 equal round plates in 3 rows of 3. The second tray is exactly filled by 16 equal round plates in 4 rows of 4. In each tray the plates touch each other and the sides. How much longer is the radius of a plate in the first tray than in the second tray?
hints: In each tray, the plates in one row share the 24 cm side equally. Find each plate's diameter, then its radius.
In the first tray, 3 plates fit across 24 cm. Find the diameter of one plate: 24 divided by 3.
Example: A 20 cm square tray holds 2 plates across, so each is 10 cm wide with radius 5 cm. If it holds 5 plates across, each is 4 cm wide with radius 2 cm. The radii differ by 5 - 2 = 3 cm.

stepByStep.text: First tray: 3 plates across.
So the radius of a plate in the first tray is 4 cm.
Second tray: 4 plates across.
So the radius of a plate in the second tray is 3 cm.
Compare the radii.
The radius in the first tray is longer by 1 cm.

misconceptions.A: This compares the diameters, 8 cm and 6 cm. The question asks about the radii, 4 cm and 3 cm.
misconceptions.B: 3 cm is the radius of a plate in the second tray. Compare it with the radius in the first tray, 4 cm.
misconceptions.C: Great work! The radii are 4 cm and 3 cm, so the difference is 1 cm.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two radii. To find how much longer, subtract.

questionText: A wire 132 cm long is cut into 3 equal pieces. Each piece is bent to make a circle. What is the radius of each circle? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Each piece of wire becomes the distance around one circle. Find the length of one piece first.
Divide 132 cm by 3 to find the length of one piece.
Example: A wire 176 cm long is cut into 2 equal pieces of 88 cm. For a circle, 44/7 times the radius is 88, so the radius is 14 cm.

stepByStep.text: Length of one piece.
This is the circumference of one circle: 2 times 22/7 times the radius is 44.
A radius of 7 cm fits.
The radius of each circle is 7 cm.

misconceptions.A: 14 cm is the diameter of each circle. The radius is half of it.
misconceptions.B: This is the radius if the whole 132 cm wire made one circle. The wire is first cut into 3 equal pieces.
misconceptions.C: 44 cm is the length of one piece, which is the circumference. Use it to find the radius.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Each piece is 44 cm, and a circle of radius 7 cm has circumference 44 cm.

questionText: Twelve equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 3 rows of 4. Each circle touches the circles next to it, and the circles on the outside touch the sides of the rectangle. The area of the rectangle is 432 sq cm. What is the radius of each circle?
hints: Each circle sits snugly inside its own little square, and the twelve little squares fill the rectangle exactly. Work backwards from the area.
Share the area of the rectangle equally among the 12 little squares. Then find the side of one little square, and think about how that side is related to the circle inside it.

Similar problem: 6 equal circles in 2 rows of 3 fill a rectangle of area 96 sq cm. Each little square has area 96 ÷ 6 = 16 sq cm, so its side is 4 cm. That side is the diameter of a circle, so the radius is 2 cm.

stepByStep.text: The rectangle is made of 12 equal little squares, one around each circle.
A square of area 36 sq cm has a side of 6 cm.
The side of the little square is the diameter of the circle inside it.
The radius is half the diameter.
So the radius of each circle is 3 cm.

misconceptions.A: 6 cm is the side of each little square, which is the diameter of a circle. The question asks for the radius.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Each circle fits a 6 cm square, so its diameter is 6 cm and its radius is 3 cm.
misconceptions.C: Check with a radius of 9 cm: the rectangle would be 72 cm by 54 cm, far bigger than 432 sq cm.
misconceptions.D: Check with a radius of 12 cm: four circles side by side would already be 96 cm long. Try sharing the area among 12 little squares.

questionText: A round pond has a radius of 7 m. A path 7 m wide runs all the way around the pond. What is the area of the path? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: The path is a ring. A ring is what is left when a small circle is taken out of a bigger circle with the same centre.
Find the radius of the big circle made by the pond and the path together. It reaches from the centre of the pond to the outer edge of the path.

Similar problem: a pond of radius 14 m with a path 7 m wide. The big circle has radius 21 m and area 22/7 x 21 x 21 = 1386 sq m. The pond has area 22/7 x 14 x 14 = 616 sq m. The path is 1386 - 616 = 770 sq m.

stepByStep.text: The pond and path together make a big circle. Find its radius.
Find the area of the big circle.
Find the area of the pond.
Take the pond out of the big circle.
So the area of the path is 462 sq m.

misconceptions.A: This is the area of a circle of radius 7 m, which is the pond. The path is the ring around it, out to 14 m from the centre.
misconceptions.B: This is the area of the pond and the path together. Take the area of the pond away.
misconceptions.C: Great work! The big circle is 616 sq m, the pond is 154 sq m, and 616 - 154 = 462.
misconceptions.D: The path is not twice the pond. Find the big circle of radius 14 m and take the pond away from it.

questionText: When the radius of a circle is made twice as long, its circumference becomes 88 cm longer than before. What was the radius of the circle at the start? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Think about what happens to the circumference when the radius is doubled. You can also test each choice: find the circumference before and after, and see how much it grows.
Try a radius of 7 cm. The circumference is 44 cm. With a radius of 14 cm it is 88 cm. Find how much it has grown, and compare with what the question says.

Similar problem: doubling the radius makes the circumference 132 cm longer. Doubling the radius doubles the circumference, so the extra part equals the old circumference, 132 cm. Since 2 x 22/7 x 21 = 132, the radius at the start was 21 cm.

stepByStep.text: When the radius is doubled, the circumference is doubled too.
So the extra length is exactly as long as the old circumference: the old circumference is 88 cm.
Find the radius of a circle with circumference 88 cm.
Check: the new radius is 28 cm, and the circumference has grown by 88 cm.
So the radius at the start was 14 cm.

misconceptions.A: Test it: with 7 cm the circumference is 44 cm, and with 14 cm it is 88 cm. It grows by only 44 cm. Here 88 cm is the extra length, not the new circumference.
misconceptions.B: 28 cm is the radius after doubling. The question asks for the radius at the start.
misconceptions.C: This halves 88. Try finding the circumference for each radius and see how much it grows when the radius is doubled.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The circumference goes from 88 cm to 176 cm, which is 88 cm longer.

questionText: Seven points are marked on a circle. Each point is joined by a straight chord to every other point, except the two points right next to it. How many chords are drawn?
hints: Work out how many chords leave one point. Then think carefully before you multiply: every chord has two ends.
From one point there are 6 other points. Two of them are its neighbours, so find how many chords start at this point.

Similar problem: five points on a circle, each joined to every point except its two neighbours. Each point sends out 2 chords, and 5 x 2 = 10. But every chord has been counted from both of its ends, so there are 10 ÷ 2 = 5 chords.

stepByStep.text: From each point, take away the point itself and its two neighbours.
Seven points each send out 4 chords.
Each chord joins two points, so it has been counted twice.
Halve the total.
So 14 chords are drawn.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Each point sends out 4 chords, and halving 7 x 4 gives 14.
misconceptions.B: This is 7 x 4. Each chord joins two points, so it has been counted once from each end.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of chords when every pair of points is joined. Here the points right next to each other are not joined.
misconceptions.D: These are the 7 short joins between neighbours, which are the ones left out. Count the other chords.

questionText: Eight points are marked on a circle, equally spaced all the way round. Every pair of points is joined by a chord. How many of these chords are NOT diameters of the circle?
hints: Count all the chords first, in an orderly way. Then decide which chords pass through the centre, and be careful not to count any of those twice.
The first point is joined to 7 others, the second to 6 new ones, and so on. A chord is a diameter only when it joins a point to the point exactly opposite.

Similar problem: six equally spaced points. The chords number 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. The six points make 3 opposite pairs, so 3 chords are diameters. That leaves 15 - 3 = 12 chords that are not diameters.

stepByStep.text: Count all the chords.
A chord is a diameter when it joins two opposite points.
Eight points make 4 opposite pairs, so there are 4 diameters.
Take the diameters away from all the chords.
So 24 of the chords are not diameters.

misconceptions.A: This takes away 8 diameters, one for each point. Each diameter joins two opposite points, so 8 points share only 4 diameters.
misconceptions.B: Exactly! There are 28 chords, 4 of them are diameters, and 28 - 4 = 24.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of all the chords. Some of them pass through the centre, and those must be left out.
misconceptions.D: 4 is the number of diameters. The question asks for the chords that are not diameters.

questionText: A small circle is drawn inside a big circle. The small circle touches the big circle at exactly one point, and it also passes through the centre of the big circle. The diameter of the big circle is 24 cm. How far apart are the centres of the two circles?
hints: Imagine a straight line from the point where the circles touch to the centre of the big circle. Think about what this line is for each of the two circles.
That line is a radius of the big circle. It also goes right across the small circle, from one side to the other through its centre.

Similar problem: the big circle has diameter 40 cm. Its radius is 20 cm, and this is the diameter of the small circle. The small circle's centre is halfway along, 10 cm from the big centre. So the centres are 10 cm apart.

stepByStep.text: Find the radius of the big circle.
The line from the touching point to the big centre is 12 cm long, and it is a diameter of the small circle.
The centre of the small circle is halfway along this line.
So the small centre is 6 cm from the big centre.
So the centres of the two circles are 6 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: Lovely! The small circle's diameter is 12 cm, so its centre is 6 cm from the centre of the big circle.
misconceptions.B: 12 cm is the radius of the big circle, and the whole width of the small circle. The small circle's centre is only halfway along it.
misconceptions.C: 18 cm is how far the small centre is from the far side of the big circle. Measure from centre to centre.
misconceptions.D: This halves once too often. The small circle's diameter is 12 cm and its radius is 6 cm.

questionText: Three coins of different sizes lie flat on a table, and each coin touches the other two. The distances between their centres are 7 cm, 8 cm and 9 cm. What is the radius of the largest coin?
hints: When two coins touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius. Think about what you get if you add all three distances.
Add 7, 8 and 9. In that total every radius has been counted twice. Halve it to find the three radii added together.
Similar problem: the distances are 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. They add up to 18 cm, so the three radii add up to 9 cm. The two smaller coins are 5 cm apart, so the largest coin has radius 9 - 5 = 4 cm.

stepByStep.text: Add the three distances. Each radius is counted twice.
Halve to get the three radii added together.
The two smaller coins have the closest centres, 7 cm apart. Take their radii away.
Check: the radii are 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm.
So the radius of the largest coin is 5 cm.

misconceptions.A: This halves 9 cm. That would be right for two equal coins, but these coins are all different sizes.
misconceptions.B: 4 cm is the radius of the middle coin. Check which coin is the largest: the radii are 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The radii are 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, and they give distances of 7 cm, 8 cm and 9 cm.
misconceptions.D: 9 cm is the distance between two centres. It is made of two radii added together.

questionText: Two round tins, each of radius 7 cm, stand on a table touching each other. A ribbon is pulled tight around the two tins together. It goes straight across from one tin to the other on both sides, and it curves around the outer half of each tin. How long is the ribbon? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Break the ribbon into its parts: the straight parts and the curved parts. Find each part and add them up.
Each straight part runs from the widest point of one tin to the widest point of the other, so it is as long as the distance between the two centres. The two curved parts are half circles.

Similar problem: two tins of radius 14 cm. The centres are 28 cm apart, so the two straight parts are 28 cm each. The two half circles make one whole circle of 2 x 22/7 x 14 = 88 cm. The ribbon is 28 + 28 + 88 = 144 cm long.

stepByStep.text: The tins touch, so their centres are two radii apart. Each straight part is this long.
There are two straight parts.
The two curved parts are half circles, which together make one whole circle.
Add the straight parts and the curved parts.
So the ribbon is 72 cm long.

misconceptions.A: This is the distance around both tins separately. The ribbon only curves around the outer half of each tin, and it has two straight parts.
misconceptions.B: This has only one straight part. The ribbon crosses from tin to tin on both sides.
misconceptions.C: Wonderful! Two straight parts of 14 cm and one whole circle of 44 cm make 72 cm.
misconceptions.D: Each straight part is 14 cm long, the distance between the centres, so the two together are 28 cm, not 56 cm.

questionText: The hour hand of a wall clock is 7 cm long. How far does the tip of the hour hand travel in one full day of 24 hours? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: The tip of the hand moves along a circle. Before you calculate, think about how many times the hour hand goes all the way round in a whole day.
The hour hand takes 12 hours to go once round the clock face. Work out how many times it goes round in 24 hours.
Similar problem: a minute hand 21 cm long, over 2 hours. The minute hand goes round once every hour, so twice in 2 hours. One round is 2 x 22/7 x 21 = 132 cm, so the tip travels 2 x 132 = 264 cm.

stepByStep.text: The tip moves on a circle of radius 7 cm. Find the distance once round.
The hour hand goes once round in 12 hours. Find how many times it goes round in a day.
Multiply the distance once round by the number of rounds.
So the tip of the hour hand travels 88 cm.

misconceptions.A: 44 cm is once round the clock. The hour hand goes round once every 12 hours, and a day has 24 hours.
misconceptions.B: This takes the hand round 24 times, once every hour. That is what the minute hand does. The hour hand is much slower.
misconceptions.C: This is only half a round. In 24 hours the hour hand goes all the way round, and more than once.
misconceptions.D: Great job! The hour hand goes round twice in a day, and 2 x 44 = 88.

questionText: Eight circles of equal diameters are drawn in a rectangle in 2 rows of 4. Each circle touches the circles next to it and the nearest sides of the rectangle at one point only. The radius of each circle is 6 cm. Find the perimeter of the rectangle.
hints: The circles fill the rectangle exactly, so its length and breadth can be counted in circle widths. Then go all the way round the rectangle.
Find the diameter of one circle: it is twice the radius of 6 cm. The length of the rectangle is 4 diameters and the breadth is 2 diameters.
Similar example: 6 equal circles of radius 5 cm sit in a rectangle in 2 rows of 3. The diameter is 10 cm, so the length is 30 cm and the breadth is 20 cm. The perimeter is 2 × (30 + 20) = 100 cm.

stepByStep.text: The diameter of each circle is twice the radius.
The length holds 4 circles and the breadth holds 2 circles.
Add the length and the breadth, then double it to go round all four sides.
The perimeter of the rectangle is 144 cm.

misconceptions.A: 48 + 24 = 72 is the length plus the breadth, which is only halfway round. Double it for all four sides.
misconceptions.B: 48 cm is the length of the rectangle, 4 diameters. The perimeter goes all the way round: two lengths and two breadths.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The rectangle is 48 cm by 24 cm, and 2 × (48 + 24) = 144.
misconceptions.D: 96 cm is the two lengths only, 48 + 48. Add the two breadths of 24 cm as well.

questionText: A circle has a radius of 21 cm. What is its area? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses π and the radius.
Area = π × radius × radius. Put 21 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 21 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 7 cm. Area = 22/7 × 7 × 7. First 7 ÷ 7 = 1. Then 22 × 1 × 7 = 154. The area is 154 cm².

stepByStep.text: The area of a circle is π × radius × radius. The radius is 21 cm.
Divide 21 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 22 by 3, then by 21.
The area is 1386 cm².

misconceptions.A: Yes! 22/7 × 21 × 21 = 1386, so the area is 1386 cm².
misconceptions.B: This is half of the area. Something got halved along the way. Multiply 22/7 by 21, then by 21 again.
misconceptions.C: 42 is just the diameter, 2 × 21. For the area, multiply 22/7 by the radius and by the radius again.
misconceptions.D: This is double the area. The 2 belongs to the circumference rule. The area rule is π × radius × radius, with no 2.

questionText: A circle has a radius of 35 cm. What is its circumference? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses π and the radius.
Circumference = 2 × π × radius. Put 35 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 35 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 21 cm. Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 21. First 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Then 2 × 22 × 3 = 132. The circumference is 132 cm.

stepByStep.text: The circumference of a circle is 2 × π × radius. The radius is 35 cm.
Divide 35 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 5.
The circumference is 220 cm.

misconceptions.A: 70 is just the diameter, 2 × 35. To go around the circle, multiply the diameter by 22/7 as well.
misconceptions.B: This is double the circumference. It happens if you double the radius and then multiply by 2 again. Use 2 × 22/7 × 35.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220, so the circumference is 220 cm.
misconceptions.D: This is 22/7 × 35, which leaves out the 2. The circumference is 2 × π × radius.

questionText: A circle is a set of all points that are equidistant from a fixed point called the:
hints: All points on a circle are the same distance from one special point.
This fixed point in the middle is called the centre.
The centre is NOT on the circle — it's inside it!

stepByStep.text: A circle is defined by its centre and radius.
stepByStep.latex: \text{All points at distance } r \text{ from centre}

stepByStep.text: The fixed point is the centre.

misconceptions.B: Radius is the DISTANCE from centre to circle, not the point itself
misconceptions.C: Diameter is a line segment, not a point
misconceptions.D: Chord is a line segment with endpoints on the circle

questionText: If the radius of a circle is 9.5 cm, what is its diameter?
hints: The diameter is always twice the radius.
= 19 cm

stepByStep.text: d = 2r
d = 19 cm

misconceptions.A: Multiplied by 3 instead of 2
misconceptions.B: Divided by 2 instead of multiplying (found radius from diameter)
misconceptions.D: Diameter is NOT the same as radius — it's twice the radius

questionText: The longest chord of a circle is called the:
hints: A chord is a line segment with both endpoints on the circle.
The longest possible chord passes through the centre.
A chord through the centre = diameter. It's the longest chord.

stepByStep.text: A chord through the centre is the longest chord possible.
Answer: diameter

misconceptions.A: Arc is a curved part of the circle, not a straight line segment
misconceptions.B: Circumference is the distance AROUND the circle, not a chord
misconceptions.C: Radius goes from centre to the circle — it's not a chord (both ends must be ON the circle)

questionText: How many axes of symmetry does a circle have?
hints: Every diameter divides the circle into two equal halves.
How many diameters can you draw? You can draw one in ANY direction!
Infinite diameters = infinite axes of symmetry.

stepByStep.text: Every diameter is an axis of symmetry.
Infinite diameters → infinite axes.

misconceptions.A: A circle has MORE symmetry than any polygon, not less
misconceptions.C: 2 is for a rectangle
misconceptions.D: 4 is for a square

questionText: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 21 cm. (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Circumference = 2 × π × r = 2 × 22/7 × 21.
Simplify: 21 ÷ 7 = 3. So C = 2 × 22 × 3.

stepByStep.text: Circumference = 132 cm

misconceptions.A: 66 = πr (forgot to multiply by 2, or used πd with r instead of d)
misconceptions.C: 42 = 2 × 21 (forgot π)
misconceptions.D: 264 = 2 × 132 (doubled the answer)

questionText: A circle has a radius of 28 cm. What is its area? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses π and the radius.
Area = π × radius × radius. Put 28 in for the radius and 22/7 for π. Try dividing 28 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 21 cm. Area = 22/7 × 21 × 21. First 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Then 22 × 3 × 21 = 1386. The area is 1386 cm².

stepByStep.text: The area of a circle is π × radius × radius. The radius is 28 cm.
Divide 28 by 7 first to make the sum easy.
Now multiply 22 by 4, then by 28.
The area is 2464 cm².

misconceptions.A: Yes! 22/7 × 28 × 28 = 2464, so the area is 2464 cm².
misconceptions.B: This is double the area. The 2 belongs to the circumference rule. The area rule is π × radius × radius, with no 2.
